Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A salon sells a haircut service for Rs 500. Services are not physical goods, so there is no stock quantity to count. The cashier taps Haircut and adds one service to the bill.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A shop has milk at Rs 60 each. One Branch A stock row contains 20 cartons. A customer buys 2 cartons and the cashier scans the barcode.

Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. This is the ordinary sufficient-stock sale and should be quick with no extra popup.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A plain snack costs Rs 40 but no stock row was ever received for it. The cashier can physically see 3 snacks on the counter, and this tenant allows overselling.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app uses the master product price of Rs 40 and adds quantity 3. There is no batch to reserve, so the local app does not invent stock or make stock negative. The order still records that 3 items were requested.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: This is acceptable for sales-first shops. The backend should mark these 3 items as having no physical stock allocation for audit/reporting.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A shelf item costs Rs 40 and has one matching stock row, but the system quantity is 0. The salesman is holding 2 real items and overselling is allowed.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app keeps the zero-quantity row as the identity of the item, adds quantity 2 at Rs 40, and leaves local stock at 0. It does not reduce the row to -2. The sale can continue because the business permits stock discrepancies.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No blocking is needed for your current clients. Later, a small non-blocking 'oversold 2' badge or audit reason would help managers understand the mismatch.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A strict-stock tenant has a plain product at Rs 40 with only a quantity-0 row. The cashier tries to sell 1 while ALLOW_OVERSELL is OFF.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: This is a known deferred edge case: an initial plain-product add can fall back to a normal base-price line instead of being blocked. Variant products do block correctly in strict mode.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Fix this before enabling strict stock for any client. It is safe to defer now because all current clients use ALLOW_OVERSELL ON.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The cashier works in Branch A. Shampoo has 8 units at Rs 55 in Branch B only, while the product's master price is Rs 60. A Branch A customer buys one shampoo.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app does not take Branch B stock. It can add the plain product at Branch A's master price of Rs 60 because no Branch A row matched. The tester must confirm Branch B quantity remains 8.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Keep the store separation. A future warning such as 'No Branch A stock found; using master price' would make stock-sync mistakes easier to notice.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Two same-price stock batches contain 4 and 6 rice bags at Rs 100 each. A customer buys 8 bags.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The cashier sees one cart line: Rice, quantity 8, Rs 100 each. Behind the scenes the app reserves 4 from the first batch and 4 from the second. It must not create two lines just because there are two batches at the same commercial price.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Same price means one simple customer-facing line while stock allocation stays detailed internally.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Two yogurt batches both sell at Rs 100. Four expire on 10 July and six expire on 20 July. The customer buys six.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app uses the four earlier-expiring yogurts first and then two from the later batch. The cart remains one six-unit line at Rs 100. A tester should verify the earliest expiry row is consumed before the later row.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. This is FEFO: first expiry, first out.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Rice has an old batch at Rs 100 and a newer batch at Rs 110. Both are available and the cashier scans one bag.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: Because the selling prices differ, the app opens a batch/price chooser. The cashier chooses the actual commercial price to apply before anything is added. It must not silently choose one price or blend both into one price.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. The cashier must make the pricing decision when different batches genuinely have different selling prices.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The rice price chooser opens for Rs 100 and Rs 110 batches, but the cashier taps outside it by mistake.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app adds nothing and displays 'No batch selected - item was not added to cart.' A tester should confirm there is no hidden cart line and no stock reservation after the dismissal.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. A cancelled choice must be visible so the cashier does not think the item was billed.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Two compatible stock rows sell at the same Rs 100 price. One has 10 units and the other has 5. The cashier initially asks for 20 while overselling is allowed.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app first reserves all real stock: 10 from the first row and 5 from the second. The cart displays quantity 20 at Rs 100, but only the final 5 are a shortage. Neither stock row becomes negative.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Real stock must always be consumed before only the true remainder is treated as oversold.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The cashier initially asks for 20 items. The selected Rs 100 batch has 10, but another valid batch has 5 at Rs 110. Overselling is allowed.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: Known gap: for this one-shot initial add, the app begins with the batch/price chosen by the cashier. It can oversell from the Rs 100 group instead of automatically creating a separate Rs 110 line for the other 5 available items.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: A business decision is needed before changing this: either ask the cashier to approve a split price, or automatically create separate Rs 100 and Rs 110 lines. Only the final 5 should then be oversold.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A customer already has 2 soap bars at Rs 50 in the cart. The selected stock group still has 8 available. The customer asks for 5 bars instead.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app calculates that only 3 more are needed, reserves exactly 3, and updates the same cart line from 2 to 5. The line remains at Rs 50 each.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Quantity changes should reserve only the difference, not reserve the full quantity again.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A customer wants 20 units. The current cart line's Rs 100 group can provide 10, and another valid group can provide 5 at Rs 110. The cashier increases the quantity after the first line already exists.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app consumes the remaining 10 from the Rs 100 group, creates a separate correctly-priced Rs 110 line for the available 5, and permits only the final 5 as oversold. The tester should see total quantity 20 across two price lines.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Current handling is correct. A future visual shortage label could help a cashier understand why 5 are oversold.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: All matching stock rows together have 15 units, but a customer requests 20 and overselling is allowed.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app reserves all 15 physical units first. It still lets the cart reach 20, but keeps local stock at zero rather than -5. The backend receives the full requested quantity and allocation details.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No frontend block is needed. The backend should permanently record that 15 were allocated and 5 were oversold for reporting and return handling.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: All matching stock rows together have 15 units, but the customer asks for 20 and overselling is disabled.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app refuses the unavailable increase. The cart remains at the previously valid quantity and the existing stock reservations do not change. A tester should verify that no partial accidental increase occurs.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed for strict-stock clients, apart from the separate initial plain zero-stock issue in row 5.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A saved-order restore or background flow has no dialog on screen. It needs 8 items while only 5 are locally available.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The same ALLOW_OVERSELL setting applies even without a popup. With it ON, the first 5 are reserved and the final 3 are accepted as oversold. With it OFF, the extra 3 are blocked.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Inventory policy must be identical for visible and headless flows.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A customer changes their mind: yogurt quantity goes from 3 to 2, then the cashier removes the item completely.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: When quantity falls from 3 to 2, one previously reserved yogurt returns to its original stock row. When the line is removed, the remaining two reservations return too. The tester should see stock return to its starting value.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. This prevents stock from disappearing permanently after a cart edit.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A held order reserved 4 bottles from batch A and 2 from batch B. The cashier saves it, opens another customer, then reopens the held order.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app restores the 4+2 batch allocation and the six-item cart line instead of treating it as a new unallocated sale. The tester should verify both batches are reserved again after reopening.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Retest this whenever the saved-order API or local storage format changes.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A cashier taps '+' five times quickly, then the app is closed or restarted immediately.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: Cart and stock saves are queued one after another. The newest quantity should survive; an earlier save should not finish later and overwrite it. A tester can repeat rapid adds and restart to verify the last displayed quantity returns.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No correctness change needed. Full-snapshot saves can be optimized later if performance becomes a problem.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Two cart lines use the same product but differ by variant, sale unit or batch. One old saved line is corrupt because of a previous app version.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: Every cart line has its own line ID, so valid lines remain separate and load normally. The corrupt row is skipped instead of crashing the whole cart screen.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A demo phone still exists in the catalog, but it is marked not sellable. A cashier scans its barcode.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A customer brings a new imported biscuit with barcode 123, but the product has not yet been created in the local catalog.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A catalog mistake gives barcode 123 to two different products or variants. The cashier scans 123.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app reports an ambiguous barcode and does not choose the first record. The tester should confirm neither product is automatically added.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A weighing-scale label represents 1.250 KG of meat. Meat costs Rs 400 per KG, so the expected line amount is Rs 500.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The scanner passes the decimal quantity 1.250 through the cart flow. The cart should show 1.250 KG and calculate Rs 500, not round it to 1 KG or 2 KG.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A damaged scale barcode should contain 1.250 KG, but its embedded quantity digits are unreadable.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The current fallback can add quantity 1 instead of clearly telling the cashier that the barcode quantity failed. This could charge the wrong amount for weighed goods.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A newly imported item has no selling price yet, so its catalog price is Rs 0. The cashier enters Rs 75 and quantity 2 in the quick-entry window.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app opens the quick price/quantity window before adding. After confirmation, the cart contains quantity 2 at Rs 75 each. A tester should verify the total is Rs 150.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The same zero-price quick-entry window is opened, but the cashier presses Cancel because they do not know the price.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The product is not added and the app clearly says 'Price not entered - item was not added to cart.' The tester should verify the cart and stock remain unchanged.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A regular customer previously paid Rs 80 for sugar, but the current minimum permitted price is Rs 90.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A cashier negotiates a floor fan from Rs 1,000 down to Rs 900. The customer asks for a second fan and the cashier scans the same product again.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A t-shirt product has Red/S at Rs 450, Red/M at Rs 500 and Blue/M at Rs 520. The cashier sells Red/M.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app either shows the variant picker or resolves the exact variant from its barcode. The cart stores Red/M's variant ID and attributes, so it is not confused with Red/S or Blue/M.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Test picker selection and each variant barcode separately.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A perfume has exactly one active variant: Standard 50ml at Rs 300. The cashier taps the product tile.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app selects Standard 50ml automatically and adds it as a variant line. It should not make the cashier perform an unnecessary extra picker tap for a single possible choice.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Red/M has an exact stock row with quantity 0, Blue/M has 10, and overselling is enabled. The customer physically has a Red/M shirt.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app sells Red/M using its exact zero-quantity row and leaves that row at 0. It never uses the 10 Blue/M units. If the Red/M row is missing completely, row 34 applies: the sale is still allowed with no allocation.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Overselling allows a shortage for the requested identity; it never substitutes a different variant.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Red/M has no stock row at all, although Blue/M has 10 and the plain product has general stock 20. The customer is physically holding a Red/M item and overselling is enabled.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app now adds Red/M using its exact variant ID with no stock allocation. It does not borrow Blue/M or general stock, and local Blue/M quantity remains 10. Checkout carries the requested Red/M quantity as unallocated oversell.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No blocking is needed when overselling is enabled. The backend must accept a variant-level oversell with stock_id null and record the unallocated quantity.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Variants are enabled for a shoe product, but every colour/size variant was deactivated by an admin.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app reports that there are no active variants and does not sell the shoe as a plain generic item. The tester should confirm no stock is deducted.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Backend must keep sending the persistent variant-mode flag so an empty active list cannot accidentally make a variant product look plain.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A Red shirt costs Rs 12 per piece. A CASE is 12 pieces. No special CASE price is configured, and the customer buys one CASE.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app starts with the Red variant price: 12 x Rs 12 = Rs 144 for the CASE. Internally it stores the base price per piece but displays and sends Rs 144 per CASE.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. This is the expected fallback when no explicit sale-unit price exists.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The same Red shirt costs Rs 12 per piece, but the product's CASE master price is Rs 100 for every colour. The customer buys one Red CASE.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The explicit CASE price wins over the simple 12 x Rs 12 calculation. The cart and checkout show one Red CASE at Rs 100.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed when the business intends one common CASE price for all variants.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The business wants Red CASE at Rs 110 and Blue CASE at Rs 130. Both CASEs contain 12 pieces.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The current product master data has no separate price table directly keyed by both variant and sale unit. This can work only if the backend provides a CASE price override on each variant's own stock row.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Add a true variant-plus-sale-unit pricing contract later if per-stock overrides cannot cover the business need.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Red stock has a CASE price override of Rs 110. Product CASE master price is Rs 100 and Red piece price is Rs 12.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The selected Red stock row's CASE override has the highest priority, so one Red CASE sells for Rs 110. The tester should verify Rs 110 is used instead of Rs 100 or Rs 144.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. This is the intended priority for a batch/variant-specific commercial price.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: One CASE equals 12 pieces. Stock has 20 pieces and a customer buys 1 CASE.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The cart displays quantity 1 CASE, while the internal stock reservation consumes 12 pieces. Checkout sends the sale unit and one CASE quantity at the correct CASE price.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. Tester should verify display quantity and stock quantity are deliberately in different units.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: One CASE equals 12 pieces, but the selected stock has only 8 pieces. Overselling is enabled and the customer physically has a full CASE.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app reserves the available 8 pieces, accepts the remaining 4 as shortage, and still displays one CASE. Local stock stops at 0; it must not show -4.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No frontend block is needed. Backend reports should distinguish 8 allocated pieces from 4 oversold pieces.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The cart currently shows 5 PCS. The cashier changes its unit to CASE, where one CASE equals 12 PCS.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The current business meaning preserves the visible number: 5 PCS becomes 5 CASE, so the line now needs 60 base pieces. The app reserves the extra stock or restores stock when changing back.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Keep this behaviour documented in the UI. It is intentional, but cashiers may otherwise expect 5 PCS to become 0.4167 CASE.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A restaurant/server cart contains 1.5 KG of fish at Rs 200 per KG. The cashier changes it first to 2.0 KG and then to 1.25 KG.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: Fixed behaviour: increasing to 2.0 sends an extra 0.5 KG; reducing to 1.25 sends 1.25 KG. The old integer conversion no longer turns 0.5 into 0. No API call is made if the quantity did not actually change.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Frontend handling is correct now. The restaurant backend must continue accepting decimal quantities for KG, LTR and similar units.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The base product minimum price is Rs 100, but a clearance Red variant is intentionally allowed to sell at Rs 80.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: Known gap: the minimum-price calculation currently looks at the base product's floor. It can reject a valid Rs 80 Red-variant price and force it back up to Rs 100.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Make the minimum-price/margin calculation aware of the selected variant before using lower-priced clearance variants.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A Green/M hoodie is added at Rs 500 and saved in a held order. Before it is reopened, an admin deactivates Green/M.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The existing held cart line keeps its saved Green/M identity and Rs 500 price. A new sale cannot select that inactive variant. The tester should confirm the held order does not silently become a base-product price.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed. This protects the price already agreed in an open order while blocking new sales of deactivated variants.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A sale contains Blue/L, two CASEs at Rs 120 per CASE, with stock taken from IDs 11 and 12. Some requested quantity may be oversold.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: Checkout includes the product ID, Blue/L variant ID, CASE sale-unit ID, quantity, price and stock allocation identities. The total requested quantity remains complete even when local stock could allocate only part of it.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Backend must make the final authoritative stock decision, persist exact allocations, and record any oversold remainder.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: Register A and Register B both see stock 10. A completes a sale of 8 first. B then tries to complete another sale of 8.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The frontend prevents repeated tapping on one screen and now preserves the backend's structured conflict message. But B's device cannot know A changed stock until the backend checks it.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Backend must use one transaction/atomic allocation plus an idempotency key. With overselling ON, it should allocate B the remaining 2 and audit the other 6 as oversold.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A customer buys a T-Shirt Red/L at Rs 500 and asks for a simplified tax invoice PDF.

Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: No change needed for the main simplified PDF. Test every other tenant-specific or thermal layout separately if it is used.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A customer returns Black/38 jeans originally sold for Rs 1,200. The return clerk needs to confirm the exact size and colour.

Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Add the variant text to every printed return summary if staff use those documents to verify returned goods.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: An admin creates Red/S, Red/M and Blue/M t-shirt variants. Later they delete Red/S, add Blue/L and change Red/M from Rs 500 to Rs 550.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The app sends new, changed and deleted variant rows together and rejects duplicate colour/size combinations or duplicate barcodes. Variant property choices such as COLOR and SIZE are loaded from the product-properties API.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Validate the live product-properties API response and show an admin-visible error if it fails. Silent empty dropdowns would make variant setup confusing.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: The backend says Blue/L has 20 units globally but only 3 are available in the cashier's active store.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The variant picker and local availability use the active-store number 3, not the global number 20. A tester should confirm the store-specific quantity controls the out-of-stock display.
Ideal / Real-World Needed Improvements: Backend must consistently return active-store available quantity and the persistent variant-mode flag.

Real-World Example (with price / stock e: A head-office admin changes which fields define a stock price group while a cashier already has an open cart. The cashier scans the same paint again.
Current Way of Handling (with same examp: The later scan can appear as a second cart line because grouping is recalculated with the newest settings, although the total amount remains correct. This is confusing but not a wrong-total bug.
